story.title: The Panel's Last Word
story.place: my office, where I am writing the Panel's report
story.goalShort: I want to tell them plainly that owning the bomb will not keep us safe.
story.goalFull: I want the Panel's verdict to reach the Secretary of War: there is no defense against this bomb, only ending war. I want it there before Washington mistakes owning the bomb for safety.

facts: I spent much of the weekend drafting the Panel's final report to Secretary Stimson.
I wrote it plainly: “it is our firm opinion that no military countermeasures will be found which will be adequately effective in preventing the delivery of atomic weapons.”
I added that these devices, already vastly destructive, will only become bigger and more lethal.
Ernest arrived the weekend after Nagasaki and found me weary, morose and full of qualms about what had happened.
We fell to arguing about the bomb, and he was reminded that he had argued for a demonstration and I had blocked it.
I stung him with a biting remark that he cared only for the rich and powerful.
He tried to reassure me that because the bomb is so terrible, it will never be used again. I wasn't reassured.

I wrote that “we are not only unable to outline a program that would assure to this nation for the next decades hegemony in the field of atomic weapons; we are equally unable to insure that such hegemony, if achieved, could protect us from the most terrible destruction.”

I closed with: “We believe that the safety of this nation—as opposed to its ability to inflict damage on an enemy power—cannot lie wholly or even primarily in its scientific or technical prowess. It can be based only on making future wars impossible.”
Only three days after America's victory, I was telling Stimson and the President that the nation had no defense against these new weapons.
That week I hand-carried the letter to Washington, D.C., myself.
I met with Vannevar Bush and with George Harrison, Stimson's aide in the War Department.

steps.title: Write that no defense will be found
steps.userSide: Your Step: the first part of your Goal.
steps.whyHard: Everything I write will be read by men who must act on it, and I am not sure they will want to hear it. I have to be plain without sounding like a prophet.

steps.title: Argue it out with Ernest
steps.userSide: Your Step: the second part of your Goal.
steps.whyHard: I wrote the warning plainly, but I'm worn out and not sure I believe my own calm. Anyone who pushes back on it will find me thin-skinned.

steps.title: Close the report on safety
steps.userSide: Your Step: the third part of your Goal.
steps.whyHard: Ernest tried to comfort me and it didn't work, so I go back to the page unsettled. I have to say what the bomb means for the country without letting my mood write it.

steps.title: Carry the report to Washington
steps.userSide: Your Step: the last part of your Goal.
steps.whyHard: The report is written, but a page in a drawer protects no one. I have to put it in the right hands myself, and I don't yet know whether those hands will take it seriously.
